tldr: A humanoid control framework that geometrically adapts flat-ground, unloaded human motion data to sloped terrain and required end-effector loads, enabling sloped walking and push-pull manipulation simultaneously without any additional sensors.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of BRACE. On the left, flat-ground motion is geometrically adapted to the terrain (height map) and target wrench. On the top right, two privileged teachers are trained via reinforcement learning for force exertion and force compensation. On the bottom right, both teachers are distilled into a single, proprioception-only flow-matching student model that requires no exteroceptive sensors.
overview:
Tracking human motion captured from mocap or video has become the standard way to drive humanoid robots. However, existing motion datasets are almost entirely recorded on flat ground while carrying nothing. When a robot tries to push a heavy cart uphill or exert force with tools, the flat reference trajectory conflicts directly with the real-world slope and task loads, causing the robot to lose balance and fall.

To solve this, the authors propose a new angle: rather than forcing the controller to absorb all the disturbance, geometrically and dynamically adapt the reference trajectory itself beforehand. By synthesizing "terrain conformance" (which lifts footholds and root height to match sloped ground) with "wrench transformation" (which shifts the center of mass to brace against reaction forces), BRACE generates feasible, balanced whole-body reference poses. Furthermore, two privileged expert teachers—one for exerting forces and one for compensating external disturbances—are trained and then distilled via DAgger into a single flow-matching student model.

Evaluated on the Unitree G1 in simulation and real-world experiments, BRACE handles external disturbance forces up to 20 N, exerts forces up to 9 N, and tracks references on slopes up to 17.7 degrees. It reduces global position drift by an average of 40% and boosts task success rate by 18.25 percentage points compared to prior tracking methods. Crucially, it requires no exteroceptive sensors or force sensors; an operator can simply provide standard flat-ground motion, and the robot resolves slopes and loads entirely onboard.
contributions: Proposed a reference adaptation framework that geometrically and analytically transforms flat-ground, unloaded reference trajectories to match local terrain profiles and target end-effector wrenches (6-DoF forces and torques).
Formulated a joint solution for hand lead displacements and center-of-mass (CoM) bracing under feasibility constraints such as joint torque limits and the support polygon.
Unified two contrasting behaviors—force exertion and force compensation—from separate privileged teachers into a single flow-matching student model using DAgger.

Deployed a proprioception-only policy onto the real Unitree G1 humanoid that infers terrain and external forces without height maps or wrist force sensors, demonstrating applications in remote teleoperation and VLA learning.

sections.heading: Flat-ground motions cannot handle slopes or heavy labor
sections.summary: While whole-body tracking has become the standard interface for humanoid teleoperation and data collection, recorded motions lack elevation and contact force information. Existing methods either tackle force control or terrain tracking alone, leading to reference conflicts when both are needed. BRACE resolves this fundamental contradiction by dynamically adapting the reference trajectory.
sections.details:
Retargeting and tracking human motion capture data has gained wide adoption for humanoid control. However, there is a fundamental omission: humans in these datasets move on flat ground while carrying nothing.

Real-world tasks require pushing doors open, carrying heavy loads, or walking up sloped ramps. These motions are defined by end-effector wrenches (force $F$ and torque $\tau$) and uneven ground underneath. Feeding flat-ground, unloaded trajectories directly into a robot leads to several failures:

- Pushing against an object requires driving the hand into the contact surface, but moving only the arm causes reaction forces that destabilize balance.
- On a slope, flat-ground foot placements and root heights cause feet to scuff or trip.
- Forcing a reinforcement learning policy to resolve these discrepancies via rewards causes tracking rewards and force-exertion rewards to clash directly, destabilizing training.

BRACE (Body Reference Adaptation for Contact and Elevation) addresses this by analytically rewriting the reference trajectory itself according to terrain geometry and wrench demands. By tracking this adapted target, the robot naturally leans in and pushes forward. In Isaac Lab simulations and real-world Unitree G1 experiments, BRACE reduced global drift by 40% on average and raised success rates by 18.25 percentage points.

sections.heading: Bridging the gap between force control and whole-body tracking
sections.summary: Existing whole-body tracking either treats external forces as disturbances to reject or focuses only on static payload carrying. Meanwhile, mobile manipulation force controllers command end-effector wrenches without constraining the full-body pose. BRACE bridges this gap by combining dense whole-body tracking with both active force exertion and compensation in a single policy.
sections.details:
Prior work on humanoid control falls into three main categories:

### II-A Terrain Adaptation and Payload Tracking
RL-based motion tracking has advanced rapidly. Frameworks like Any2Track adapt to rough terrain without exteroception, while HEFT tracks human references while carrying loads. However, HEFT only considers static gravitational loads, and Any2Track treats external forces as unmodeled disturbances to reject. Neither provides a control interface to actively push a commanded force into the environment.

### II-B Force Control on Mobile Robots
Force control on legged platforms spans two directions: active force exertion and force compensation against disturbances. Frameworks like UNIFP and FACET accept end-effector wrenches or impedance commands, but they only govern base velocity and hand positions without constraining dense whole-body poses. Conversely, methods like FALCON and KinAware decouple the upper and lower body to withstand forces, but they do not track prescribed whole-body trajectories. BRACE differs by tightly maintaining whole-body reference tracking while simultaneously exerting or compensating forces.

### II-C Multi-Teacher Distillation and Behavioral Models
Recent work like HOVER and OmniXtreme distills multiple skill experts into a single policy, diffusion model, or flow-matching model. BRACE builds on this concept by distilling two conflicting behaviors—an exertion teacher pushing forward and a compensation teacher bracing against forces—into a single flow-matching student using DAgger, even though both operate from similar joint configurations.

sections.heading: Fixing references via geometry and distilling two teachers into one
sections.summary: Flat-ground motions are converted into new reference poses using terrain adaptation (lifting feet and hips along surface elevation) and wrench transformation (solving torque limits, hand displacements, and CoM shifts). Using these references, two privileged RL teachers are trained: Teacher-E for exertion and Teacher-C for compensation. Finally, DAgger distills both teachers into a proprioception-only flow-matching student.
sections.details:
The BRACE pipeline consists of three stages: reference trajectory synthesis, privileged teacher training, and distillation into a student model.

### III-A Reference Adaptation for Terrain and Wrench
From human flat-ground reference $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and target hand wrench $w_{\mathrm{cmd}} = [F; M]$, BRACE creates a geometrically and dynamically consistent target $x^\star$.

- Terrain Conformance ($\mathcal{T}$): Reading height map $\mathcal{H}$, it raises foot height $z_f$ while maintaining horizontal foot placements. It preserves swing clearance, aligns foot orientations with surface normals, and adjusts root height. Solving whole-body inverse kinematics (IK) yields the terrain-adapted trajectory $x_{\mathrm{ref}}^T$.
- Wrench Transformation ($\mathcal{F}$): Computes hand lead and body bracing in three steps:
  1. Feasibility Limits: Using arm Jacobians $J_p, J_r$, the target wrench is clamped so joint torques stay within budget $\tau^{\mathrm{budget}}$ with margin $\gamma=0.7$, producing feasible wrench $w^\star$. Center of pressure (CoP) shifts are also bounded within the support polygon.
  2. Hand Lead: From arm joint stiffness and damping, hand stiffness $k_F$ is calculated along the force direction. A displacement $\delta_p = F^\star / k_F$ is added to the hand target to generate target force $F^\star$.
  3. CoM Bracing: To cancel the reaction moment at the feet, a horizontal center-of-mass shift $\Delta c = -(\sum (p_h - c_{\mathrm{cop}}) \times F^\star + M^\star) \times \hat{z} / (mg)$ is computed to lean the torso forward. A fraction of this shift is also shared with the hand target, and whole-body IK yields the exertion target $x_E^\star$.

### III-B Privileged Teacher Policy Training
Teachers receive complete simulator state information (height maps and contact forces) as privileged observations.

- Teacher-E (Exertion): A virtual wrench field (spring-damper) is placed at the hand to generate reaction forces proportional to penetration. It is trained with tracking rewards for $x_E^\star$ and wrench accuracy rewards against $w^\star$.
- Teacher-C (Compensation): Subjected to random triangle-wave disturbance wrenches (up to 20 N), it is trained to maintain the terrain-conformed pose $x_C^\star = x_{\mathrm{ref}}^T$ without collapsing.

### III-C Distillation into a Flow-Matching Student
Real humanoids lack height maps and wrist force sensors. Therefore, the student policy takes only a history of proprioception $s_p$ (joint positions, velocities, IMU gyro, gravity vector) and is trained via DAgger.

Because force exertion and disturbance compensation demand opposite torque outputs from near-identical joint configurations, the action distribution is multimodal. BRACE uses a flow-matching network as the student backbone to prevent mode averaging and maintain sharp action outputs. Auxiliary heads predict surface normals and disturbance wrenches from intermediate representations to further structure the latent space.

Two privileged teacher policies are trained separately (top right). Finally, a flow-matching student policy reproduces both behaviors using proprioception alone (bottom right).

sections.heading: Superior bracing and force tracking from flat ground to steep slopes
sections.summary: Experiments on the Unitree G1 tested force compensation (0–20 N), force exertion (3–9 N), and torque exertion across flat ground and sloped terrain (up to 17.7 degrees). BRACE widened its lead over baselines as loads increased, cutting global position drift by 40% at maximum loads and reducing torque exertion error by over 30%. Real-world long-distance teleoperation and VLA deployment were also demonstrated.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 in the Isaac Lab simulator using the student model (no height maps or force sensors), matching real hardware constraints. Baselines included state-of-the-art trackers SONIC, TWIST2, Any2Track, and payload tracker HEFT.

### IV-A Benchmark Setup and Metrics
Unseen test motions from PHUMA and Bones-seed datasets were used. A trial was marked successful if it passed termination criteria (torso and limb heights within 0.25 m, torso orientation within 1 rad) and stayed within tracking bounds (horizontal root drift < 0.5 m on flat ground, 3D joint error MPJPE-G < 0.5 m on slopes).

### IV-B Force Compensation Performance
Unknown disturbance forces from 0 to 20 N were applied to the hands.

- Flat Ground: At 0 N, BRACE performed comparably to baselines like SONIC. As disturbance loads increased, baselines degraded sharply. Under the maximum 20 N load, BRACE outperformed the strongest baseline by 10.7 percentage points in success rate and reduced global position error (MPJPE-G) by 40%.
- Sloped Terrain (4.6–17.7 degrees): Differences became more pronounced. Under a 20 N load, BRACE widened its success rate lead to 22.9 percentage points and cut global error by 43%. While baselines slipped down slopes trying to enforce flat references, BRACE perceived slopes from proprioception and maintained steady footing.

### IV-C Force Exertion Performance
Robots were commanded to push against the environment with 3 to 9 N of force.

- Flat Ground: While baselines handled 3 N loads, SONIC dropped over 20 percentage points in success rate at 9 N. BRACE maintained a nearly flat success rate across 3–9 N, with 34% lower force error at 9 N than the nearest baseline.
- Sloped Terrain: Under this most demanding condition, BRACE beat the second-best baseline by 33.7 percentage points in success rate at 9 N. Global tracking error was reduced by 42% and force error by 47%.

### IV-D Torque Exertion and Real-World Applications
In hand torque exertion tests from 0.5 to 2.5 N·m (Fig. 4), BRACE lowered moment errors by 33% on flat ground and 32% on slopes. Real-robot deployments (Fig. 5) demonstrated teleoperation over ~1,000 miles (~1,600 km), real-time VR tracking, and autonomous execution of a banana-relocation task using a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model (GR00T N1.7) trained on collected demonstrations.

captions.F4: Comparison of hand torque exertion errors on flat ground (a) and sloped terrain (b). Even as commanded torque increases, BRACE (orange solid line) maintains low error growth, achieving 33% lower error on flat ground and 32% lower error on slopes compared to the closest baseline.
captions.F5: Real-world applications of BRACE. Demonstrations include VR teleoperation (top-left), autonomous VLA execution from demonstrations (top-right), gamepad-directed walking (bottom-left), and ~1,000-mile long-distance teleoperation with barbell load tracking (bottom-right).

sections.heading: Adapting references makes humanoids stronger walkers and workers
sections.summary: By geometrically transforming flat-ground references to account for terrain and hand wrenches, BRACE unites high-fidelity tracking with force control. Operating as a proprioception-only student without height maps or force sensors, it substantially cuts tracking drift under heavy loads and enables real-world teleoperation and VLA training.
sections.details:
BRACE offers an elegant answer to a core humanoid tracking challenge: how to adapt unloaded, flat-ground motion data to demanding physical contact tasks. Rather than asking the controller to fight external disturbances, it analytically rewrites the reference trajectory itself.

Through rigorous geometric adaptation constrained by joint torque limits and support polygons, combined with a distillation pipeline from two privileged teachers to a flow-matching student, the robot senses and adapts to slopes and loads using proprioception alone. Slashing position error by 40% and boosting success rates by roughly 18 percentage points under peak loads, BRACE establishes a strong new standard for tracking controllers on humanoid platforms.

takeaways: Dynamically adapting the reference trajectory rather than forcing the controller to reject disturbances prevents conflicts between tracking rewards and contact manipulation goals.
Contrasting behaviors—pushing with force versus absorbing external disturbances—can be cleanly merged from separate privileged teachers into a single student policy using flow matching.
Pairing geometric reference transformation with dynamic inference enables robust slope tracking and force control using joint proprioception alone, without external vision or 6-axis force sensors.
limitations: Terrain adaptation is limited to profiles detectable via proprioception (such as gentle slopes and small steps); it cannot handle large obstacles or stairs that require visual preview.
Maximum hand force is bounded by the Unitree G1's motor capabilities (tested up to 9 N exertion and 20 N compensation), requiring stronger hardware for heavy industrial workloads.
The paper does not provide a direct quantitative force accuracy comparison against dedicated mobile force controllers that optimize force without whole-body tracking targets.
